spec.full_target:
Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every t>0, e(·,t) is absolutely Lebesgue integrable on ℝ^n, E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. In addition E(s)=E(t) for all s,t>0; no assertion at time zero is made.

hypotheses.statement: u:ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m is jointly C^∞ (smooth) on this open domain.
For every x∈ℝ^n and every t>0, |u(x,t)|=1.
For every x∈ℝ^n and every t>0 there exists a real scalar a such that u_tt(x,t)−Δ_xu(x,t)=a u(x,t). No regularity of a selected scalar field is assumed.
For every pair of real times 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact C⊂ℝ^n such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and every r∈[s,t].

definitions.definition: u_tt(x,t)=∂u_t(x,t)/∂t, the componentwise second time derivative.

definitions.type: spatial derivative matrix field on ℝ^n × (0,∞)
definitions.definition: D_xu has columns ∂_{x_j}u for j=1,...,n, with ∂_{x_j} the componentwise partial derivative in coordinate j; ∂_{x_jx_j}u denotes its second derivative in that coordinate. Derivatives of u_t use the same convention. Its Frobenius square is |D_xu|²=Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|².

e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|². Norms and dot products throughout are Euclidean; all spatial integrals are Lebesgue integrals, written dx. Write e_t for the time partial derivative of e.
E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx, with exactly the normalization in the exercise (no factor 1/2). The guard N002 supplies absolute integrability and hence the ordinary finite real integral.

locals.declaration: Choose a scalar a with u_tt(x,t)−Δ_xu(x,t)=a u(x,t), as supplied pointwise by H005.

argument.text: Fix x∈ℝ^n and t>0. H001 gives positive finite dimensions and H002 permits all derivatives used here. By H004, u·u=1. Differentiation in time, by the ordinary product rule for the finite component sum defining the dot product, gives 2u·u_t=0, hence u·u_t=0. Choose the pointwise scalar a from H005. Then u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0. This uses no derivative or regularity of a.

Twice differentiating u·u=1 in time gives 2|u_t|²+2u·u_tt=0. For each coordinate j=1,...,n, twice differentiating in x_j similarly gives 2|∂_{x_j}u|²+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=0. Thus u·u_tt=−|u_t|² and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dot the normality equation for a with u and use |u|²=1. Finite distributivity and the definition of Δ_xu give a=u·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². The same calculation applies to every scalar satisfying that pointwise equation.

produces.statement: Every scalar a with u_tt(x,t)−Δ_xu(x,t)=a u(x,t) equals Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²−|u_t(x,t)|².

argument.text: F001 proves the two orthogonality identities at the arbitrary point. By F002 substitute the computed value of a into the pointwise normality equation from H005 to obtain u_tt−Δ_xu=(Σ_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|²)u. The scalar was chosen only at this point and is eliminated; it is not promoted to a regular scalar field. Generalizing x and t proves all clauses of N001.

locals.declaration: Choose the compact set C with u=q off C throughout J from F001.
Choose R>0 with C⊂(−R,R)^n from F002.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and set J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Both endpoints are positive and the first is strictly smaller than the second. Apply H006 to these two times to obtain a compact set outside which u=q throughout J.

produces.statement: There exists a compact C⊂ℝ^n with u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and r∈J.

argument.text: Choose such a compact C from F001. Compact subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are bounded: for example the increasing open boxes (−k,k)^n, k positive integers, cover C, and a finite subcover puts C in one such box. Enlarging its radius if needed gives a positive radius with strict containment in the open box. This also covers C empty.

Choose R as in F002 and set Q=[−R,R]^n. Its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞. The complement of compact C is open. On the open set (ℝ^n∖C)×int J the map u is the constant q by F001. H002 implies that all positive-order derivatives vanish on that open set. Thus at interior times e, e_t and each derivative product or spatial derivative of a product listed in N002 vanish outside C. Products and finite sums of smooth derivatives are continuous; in particular e and e_t are jointly continuous on the original open space-time domain.

produces.statement: Q has finite measure (2R)^n, C⊂int Q, all positive-order derivatives of u vanish on (ℝ^n∖C)×int J, and e,e_t and the derivative products specified in N002 are jointly continuous and zero outside C at interior times.

argument.text: At any r∈int J, each spatial function in question is continuous, hence Lebesgue measurable, and bounded on compact Q. Its absolute value is bounded by a finite nonnegative constant times the indicator of Q, since it vanishes outside C⊂Q. The integral of that bound is the constant times (2R)^n, which is finite. This proves absolute integrability of e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), for every spatial index j. No interchange of a derivative and an integral is used here.

produces.statement: For every r∈int J all the spatial functions listed in N002 are continuous, bounded on Q, zero outside C and absolutely integrable on ℝ^n.

argument.text: Since t0∈int J, F004 in particular proves integrability of e(·,t0). Generalize the arbitrary t0 and existentially retain the compatible C,R and their box Q, together with F001–F004, to obtain precisely N002. Joint continuity of e and e_t was established in S003 using H002. The energy integral has therefore been proved finite at every positive time, before the guarded definition E is used.

locals.declaration: Choose the compact C supplied by N002 at t0.
Choose R>0 together with C as in N002 at t0, so C⊂(−R,R)^n.
Choose a finite B0≥0 bounding |e_t| on Q×[t0−η,t0+η] from F002.
Fix arbitrary x for the uniform quotient estimate.
Fix an arbitrary sequence hseq of real increments.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and take J,C,R,Q from N002 at this t0. The guarded definition E is now available. By H001 and H002, the finite product rule and equality of mixed spatial and time derivatives give, at all x and positive t, e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2Σ_{j=1}^n∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t). The products and e_t are integrable at every positive time by N002.

produces.statement: At every x∈ℝ^n,t>0, e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2Σ_{j=1}^n∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t), and these spatial integrands are integrable.

argument.text: Set η=t0/4. Then η>0 and [t0−η,t0+η]⊂int J. Joint continuity of e_t from N002 on the compact set Q×[t0−η,t0+η] gives a finite nonnegative upper bound for |e_t| there. Indeed its continuous absolute value has a bounded compact image in ℝ.

produces.statement: There exists a finite B0≥0 such that |e_t(x,r)|≤B0 for every x∈Q and r∈[t0−η,t0+η]; η>0 and this time interval is contained in int J.

argument.text: Choose B0 from F002. For arbitrary x and 0<|h|<η, apply M004 to the real function r↦e(x,r), with derivative r↦e_t(x,r), on the closed interval whose endpoints are min(t0,t0+h) and max(t0,t0+h). Smoothness gives continuity and the indicated derivative on that interval; all times lie in [t0−η,t0+η]. If a total function on ℝ is required, set it to zero at nonpositive times; this leaves this positive interval and its local derivatives unchanged. For x∈Q, M004 and F002 imply |(e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0))/h|≤B0. This is the same slope in either ordering of the endpoints. For x∉Q both densities vanish by N002, so the quotient is zero. Thus the uniform dominating function on ℝ^n is B0·1_Q. It is integrable since Q is measurable of finite measure.

produces.statement: For all x∈ℝ^n and all real h with 0<|h|<η, |(e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0))/h|≤B0·1_Q(x). The function B0·1_Q is Lebesgue integrable.

argument.text: Fix an arbitrary sequence hseq:ℕ→ℝ. Temporarily assume L1: for every k, 0<|hseq(k)|<η and hseq(k)→0. Define Fseq(k)(x)=[e(x,t0+hseq(k))−e(x,t0)]/hseq(k). Each Fseq(k) is continuous in x and hence almost everywhere strongly measurable for Lebesgue measure. F003 gives the bound |Fseq(k)(x)|≤B0·1_Q(x) for every k and x. The definition of the time derivative gives Fseq(k)(x)→e_t(x,t0) at every x, because hseq tends to zero through nonzero increments. All Fseq(k) are integrable, by the bound or by integrability of their two densities.

produces.statement: Every Fseq(k) is Lebesgue almost everywhere strongly measurable and integrable, |Fseq(k)(x)|≤B0·1_Q(x) for all k,x, and Fseq(k)(x)→e_t(x,t0) for every x.

argument.text: Apply M001 with measurable space ℝ^n, Lebesgue measure, codomain ℝ, sequence Fseq, limit x↦e_t(x,t0), and bound B0·1_Q. F003 and F004 verify all premises. It follows that ∫Fseq(k) dx→∫e_t(x,t0) dx. Since both densities are integrable by N002, linearity of the real Lebesgue integral identifies the left integral with [E(t0+hseq(k))−E(t0)]/hseq(k).

Discharge L1: F005 holds for every sequence of nonzero increments tending to zero and lying in |h|<η. This proves the full punctured limit as h→0: if it failed, there would be an ε>0 and, for each positive integer k, an increment with 0<|h|<min(η,1/k) whose quotient differs from ∫e_t(x,t0)dx by at least ε. Choosing those increments would contradict F005. Thus E is differentiable at t0 with E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0) dx. Together with F001, and generalization of arbitrary t0, this is N003. Neither the chosen support witnesses nor the test sequence escapes this conclusion.

applications.bindings: Set f(r)=e(x,r), d(r)=e_t(x,r) on positive times, extending arbitrarily by zero on nonpositive times; set the endpoints to min(t0,t0+h) and max(t0,t0+h).
hypothesis_checks: h≠0 by the stipulated 0<|h|<η, so the ordered endpoints are distinct.
H002 and the finite product definition of e give continuity on this positive interval; F002 places it inside int J.
The time derivative is e_t by definition and H002; extension at nonpositive times has no effect on this interval.

applications.bindings: Set A=ℝ^n, μ=Lebesgue measure, G=ℝ, F(k)=Fseq(k), f(x)=e_t(x,t0), b(x)=B0·1_Q(x).
hypothesis_checks: Euclidean ℝ^n carries its Borel measurable structure and Lebesgue measure; ℝ is a real normed vector space.
F004 proves continuity and hence almost everywhere strong measurability of every Fseq(k).
F003 proves integrability of B0·1_Q using finite measure of Q.
F004 gives the bound pointwise, hence almost everywhere, for each k.
F004 gives pointwise convergence at every x, hence almost everywhere.

locals.declaration: Choose the compact C from N002 at t0.
Choose R>0 together with C from N002, so C⊂(−R,R)^n.
Set Qrest=[−R,R]^(n−1), with the zero-dimensional box a singleton.
T(y,z) inserts z as coordinate j and the coordinates of y in their usual order in all remaining positions.
Fix arbitrary y∈Qrest for the one-dimensional FTC calculation.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and j∈{1,...,n}, and choose compatible J,C,R,Q from N002 at t0. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). It is smooth by H002. It is zero off C by N002. Since the compact C lies in int Q, there is a neighborhood of ∂Q disjoint from C (and if C is empty all these functions are zero everywhere). Therefore g vanishes on a neighborhood of ∂Q. The product rule gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u at time t0. All three derivative integrands are integrable by N002.

produces.statement: g is smooth and zero on a neighborhood of ∂Q; ∂_{x_j}g(x)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0). Each summand and ∂_{x_j}g is absolutely integrable and zero outside C.

argument.text: Let Qrest=[−R,R]^(n−1), and let T(y,z) insert z into coordinate j, keeping the other coordinates in their original order. Set Hfun(y,z)=∂_{x_j}g(T(y,z)). The coordinate permutation identifies Q with Qrest×[−R,R] and Lebesgue integration on Q with integration for the product of Lebesgue measure restricted to Qrest and Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R]. This follows from the Cartesian product definition of Euclidean Lebesgue measure: rectangles have the product of their side lengths, invariant under coordinate reordering; that determines this measure. If n=1 the remaining factor ℝ^0 is a singleton with mass one, so the same identification applies. Both restricted measures are finite, hence s-finite. Hfun is continuous and bounded on this compact product; the product measure is finite, so Hfun is integrable there. For each fixed y∈Qrest, z↦g(T(y,z)) is smooth with derivative Hfun(y,z). Its derivative is bounded on [−R,R], hence interval integrable, and its endpoint values are zero by F001.

produces.statement: The restricted Lebesgue measures on Qrest and [−R,R] are finite and their product, transported by T, is Lebesgue measure on Q. Hfun is integrable for that product. For every y∈Qrest, the function z↦g(T(y,z)) is continuous on [−R,R], has derivative Hfun(y,z) in its interior, this derivative is interval integrable, and g(T(y,−R))=g(T(y,R))=0.

argument.text: For arbitrary y∈Qrest apply M003 with codomain ℝ, endpoints −R,R, f(z)=g(T(y,z)), and derivative d(z)=Hfun(y,z). R>0 and F002 give the ordering, continuity, derivative and integrability premises. It follows that ∫_{−R}^{R}Hfun(y,z) dz=g(T(y,R))−g(T(y,−R))=0. Since endpoints have one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero, the interval integral equals the integral for Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R]. Generalize y.

produces.statement: For every y∈Qrest the integral of Hfun(y,z) against Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R] is zero.

argument.text: Apply M002 to Hfun with outer measure Lebesgue measure restricted to Qrest and inner measure Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], codomain ℝ. F002 proves product integrability and s-finiteness. The iterated integral is zero by F003. Fubini therefore gives zero for the product integral, and the coordinate identification in F002 gives ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=0. This holds also in the singleton outer factor when n=1.

By F001 the derivative and both product summands vanish outside Q, so their whole-space integrals equal their integrals over Q. Integrate the product identity in F001, using absolute integrability and linearity. F004 gives 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, at time t0. Symmetry of the Euclidean dot product gives the asserted identity with ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t on the left. Generalize t0 and j to obtain N004, including the integrability clauses.

applications.bindings: Set V=ℝ, a=−R, b=R, f(z)=g(T(y,z)), d(z)=Hfun(y,z).
hypothesis_checks: ℝ is a complete real normed vector space.
F002 establishes continuity of z↦g(T(y,z)) on [−R,R].
F002 establishes its derivative Hfun(y,z) at each interior point.
F002 proves interval integrability of the derivative by continuity and boundedness on the compact interval.

applications.bindings: Set A=ℝ^(n−1), B=ℝ, μ=Lebesgue measure restricted to Qrest, ν=Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], V=ℝ and f(y)(z)=Hfun(y,z).
hypothesis_checks: The Euclidean factors have their Borel measurable structures. By F002 both restricted measures are finite, hence s-finite, including the mass-one singleton factor for n=1; ℝ is a real normed vector space.
F002 establishes product integrability of Hfun by boundedness and measurability on the finite-measure compact box.

argument.text: Fix t0>0. N002 proves integrability of e(·,t0) and of all product terms below, so E is the actual finite integral. N003 proves its differentiability and gives E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0) dx with e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_{j=1}^n∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. Substitute this identity, use linearity and interchange the finite sum and integral (H001 gives a finite dimension), and apply N004 to each j. This yields E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·u_tt dx−2Σ_{j=1}^n∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu) dx, all fields evaluated at t0.

produces.statement: E is differentiable at t0 and E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)−Δ_xu(x,t0)) dx.

argument.text: By N001 the final integrand in F001 is zero at every x, so E'(t0)=0. Since t0 was arbitrary, N002 and N003 together prove the complete target: e(·,t) is integrable and E is differentiable with E'(t)=0 for every positive t. No time-zero value or limiting assertion is used.

produces.statement: For every r>0, e(·,r) is integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

argument.text: To retain the final conservation statement of the supplied proof, fix s,t>0. If s<t, apply M004 to E and the zero derivative on [s,t]; extend E by zero to nonpositive times solely to match the source's total domain. F002 gives differentiability and hence continuity at all points of this positive closed interval, and derivative zero in its interior. The theorem gives slope zero and therefore E(t)=E(s). If t<s use the same application with the endpoints interchanged, and if s=t equality is immediate. Thus E is constant on (0,∞). This retains exactly the exercise's normalization.

applications.bindings: For unequal s,t, set f to E on positive times (zero elsewhere), d to the zero function, a=min(s,t), b=max(s,t).
hypothesis_checks: In the unequal-endpoint cases min(s,t)<max(s,t); the equal case is treated directly.
F002 gives differentiability and hence continuity of E at every positive time, so f is continuous on this positive interval.
F002 gives derivative zero at every positive time, including all interior points of this interval; the extension is locally equal to E there.
